questions.title: How does de novo review apply to the sufficiency of an indictment?
questions.question_body: I'm reading this opinion and the court says they review the sufficiency of an indictment 'de novo.' I'm a bit confused about what that means in this specific context. Since the district court already dismissed the indictment, is the Fifth Circuit ignoring the lower court's reasoning entirely and just looking at the indictment itself? Also, when they say they 'take the allegations as true,' does that mean the defendants can't argue that the facts are wrong at this stage?

questions.title: What is the actual distinction between the 'right-to-control' theory and 'fraudulent inducement'?
questions.question_body: I'm struggling with the court's analysis of Ciminelli. In Ciminelli, the Supreme Court rejected the 'right-to-control' theory because depriving someone of economic information isn't a traditional property interest. But in this case, the court says 'fraudulent inducement' is different. In both scenarios, the victim is being lied to so they make a bad economic decision. I don't understand why tricking someone into buying a stock is a deprivation of property, while tricking someone about a lobbyist is just a deprivation of information.

questions.title: Can a defendant be convicted of fraud if the victim suffers no actual net pecuniary loss?
questions.question_body: The defendants in this case argued that they didn't intend to 'harm' the victims, only to profit. The court cites Kousisis to say that a 'net pecuniary loss' isn't required and that providing something of equal value (like market-value securities) doesn't stop it from being fraud. This seems counterintuitive—if I trade you a $10 bill for a $10 gift card, but I lied about why I'm doing it, have I actually 'defrauded' you of property if you still have $10 of value? I'm confused about how the 'intent to defraud' element is satisfied here.

questions.title: Why is the court using mail and wire fraud precedents to interpret 18 U.S.C. § 1348?
questions.question_body: The opinion mentions that there is 'scant caselaw' regarding the specific securities fraud statute (§ 1348) in the Fifth Circuit, so they are 'borrowing' key concepts from the mail and wire fraud statutes. Is this a common interpretive tool in federal law, or is § 1348 legally linked to the mail/wire fraud statutes in a way that makes this mandatory? I'm trying to understand if the elements of § 1348 are identical to wire fraud or if the court is just using them as a helpful guide.

questions.title: How does an indictment provide a 'double jeopardy defense' against future prosecutions?
questions.question_body: In Section II, the court lists three requirements for a sufficient indictment, one of which is that it must 'provide the defendant with a double jeopardy defense against future prosecutions.' I don't understand how the wording of an indictment achieves this. Does the specificity of the charges prevent the government from charging the same conduct under a different statute later, or is this referring to something else?

questions.title: Does the 'pump and dump' mechanism inherently fit the fraudulent-inducement theory?
questions.question_body: The court concludes that the indictment is sufficient because it alleges defendants induced followers to purchase securities. In a 'pump and dump,' the fraud is usually the false hype used to inflate the price. But at the moment the follower buys the stock, they are receiving an asset. Is the 'fraudulent inducement' the lie about the stock's future value, or is the 'property deprivation' specifically the money used to buy the stock? I'm trying to figure out if the crime is the lie itself or the actual transfer of money.
